title: SC declares parts of Magna Carta of Seafarers unconstitutional. So what?
summary: The SC voids the rule that requires seafarers who had already won their labor disputes to post a bond or payment, while their shipowners or agencies are appealing the victory before a court

items: The Supreme Court declared unconstitutional a provision in the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers that required seafarers to post a bond while their shipowners appealed labor dispute victories, citing violations of due process and equal protection.

The Court also voided other provisions related to the regulation of lawyer-seafarer contracts and the use of public funds for bond premiums, emphasizing that the regulation of legal practice is under the Supreme Court's exclusive authority.
While some provisions regarding maritime education were upheld, the Court affirmed the need for reasonable regulations to ensure quality training and compliance with international standards.

The Supreme Court (SC) has declared unconstitutional a provision in the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers. Groups had previously criticized the provision as discriminatory because it requires seafarers who initially win in cases to post a bond while their shipowner or manpower agency is appealing the decision.
The High Court likewise voided other provisions in the law and other issuances related to it.

In a decision penned by Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh, the High Court en banc partially granted the five consolidated petitions challenging the legality of Republic Act (RA) No. 12021, or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers. The petitions likewise questioned certain provisions of the law’s Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR), as well as related government issuances.
Petitioners include labor lawyer Sonny Matula, several seafarers, labor organizations, and maritime educational institutions.

“The Court emphasized that although the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers was enacted to advance the welfare of Filipino seafarers, all legislative measures must conform to the Constitution. The law therefore remains valid and enforceable, except for the provisions expressly declared unconstitutional or void,” said the ruling penned by Singh.

blocks.caption: What is the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers?

blocks.text: Signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in 2024, the Magna Carta clarifies the rights of Filipino seafarers — just working conditions, right to organize, and freedom from discrimination.

The ruling voided the law’s Section 59 or the requirement for Filipino seafarers who had already won their labor disputes to post a bond or payment, while their shipowners or agencies are appealing the victory before courts. The bond requirement was supposedly meant to ensure restitution or monetary reward, should the case be subsequently reversed or modified.
Groups challenged this because the only chance for seafarers to be reimbursed for the bond they post is if they win their case.
The High Court sided with the petitioners and ruled that this bond requirement violates due process and equal protection clauses under the 1987 Constitution.
The SC said this rule imposes a financial burden on seafarers seeking to enforce favorable labor judgments, and subjects them to a disadvantage “not similarly imposed on other workers.”

“While recognizing the State’s interest in preventing ambulance chasing and protecting the maritime industry against unrestituted awards, the Court found that these objectives did not justify the challenged restriction on the execution of monetary awards,” said the SC.

The SC also declared unconstitutional the authorization to use the Department of Migrant Workers’ (DMW) Agarang Kalinga at Saklolo Para sa mga OFW na Nangangailangan (AKSYON) Fund to pay for the bond premiums. The High Court said this mechanism failed the constitutional requirement that public funds should be used for a public purpose, as found under Section 29(1), Article VI of the 1987 Constitution.

“Sections 4 and 5, Rule III of Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) Department Order No. 247, Series of 2025, were likewise declared unconstitutional and void insofar as they implemented the bond requirement,” the High Court added.

blocks.caption: SC declares parts of Magna Carta of Seafarers unconstitutional.  So what?

blocks.text: “Great, at last, our petition was resolved by the SC. This a good news. This is victory for workers especially the seafarers,” Matula told Rappler.

“We argued [that Section 59] is discriminatory. It violates the equal protection clause of the 1987 Constitution because land-based workers do not face this requirement. We also contend that it creates an unfair financial burden on sick, injured, or unemployed seafarers,” he added.

The SC also struck down Section 60 of RA No. 12021, as well as Section 4 of RA No. 10706, or the Seafarers Protection Act. The High Court said these provisions regulated the practice of law, which is a violation of Section 5(5), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution.
Petitioners challenged these sections because they regulate lawyer-seafarer contracts and cap contingent legal fees at 10%.

“Petitioners argue that this rule (Section 60) usurps the exclusive constitutional power of the Supreme Court to regulate the practice of law and may restrict seafarers’ access to competent legal counsel,” said Matula.

The SC explained that while the legislative department may create laws to protect seafarers from lawyers’ alleged abusive practices like ambulance chasing, among others, the regulation of lawyers’ professional conduct and the practice of the law remains under the High Court’s exclusive authority.
Ambulance chasing refers to the practice of lawyers of soliciting professional employment.

Apart from the said provisions, the SC also declared unconstitutional Section 1, Rule XXII, of the law’s IRR. This is because it applies Section 59 to monetary rewards from complaints filed on or after the magna carta’s effectivity.

“The Court found that the implementing provision contravened Section 94 of the law, which expressly preserves the rights, privileges and benefits previously enjoyed by Filipino seafarers before its effectivity. It reiterated that administrative regulations must conform to the statute they implement and cannot diminish rights expressly preserved by law,” said the SC.
Meanwhile, the Court denied the challenge to the law’s Sections 75, 76, and 78, because it said they do not violate constitutional guarantee of academic freedom.

items: Section 75 – States that the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) has jurisdiction over maritime education in the country.
Section 76 – Requires shipboard training for international maritime degree programs. MARINA determines the applicability of the training, including the duration.

Section 78 – Requires maritime higher educational institutions offering international maritime degree programs to have their own training ships, simulators, or related technologies. This also requires them to enter into agreements with local or international shipping companies, shipowners, or agencies for the shipboard training program of students or cadets.

blocks.text: The Philippine Association of Maritime Institutions, Inc. and other maritime educational institutions questioned these provisions before the SC.
In its ruling, the SC said academic freedom ensures the autonomy of higher educational institutions, but this freedom does not exempt them from reasonable regulations.

“[The Court] found that the challenged provisions established minimum regulatory standards intended to ensure the quality of maritime education, the competency of Filipino seafarers, and compliance with applicable international maritime standards. Particularly, the requirements relating to enrollment and available shipboard training opportunities were considered reasonable measures to address the availability of practical training for maritime students,” said the SC.
“The prohibition against charging tuition or matriculation fees for shipboard training conducted by third party providers was likewise sustained as a measure against unjustified charges,” it added.

blocks.caption: More Filipino seafarers are being abandoned at sea

blocks.text: The petitioners also questioned the legislative process leading to the magna carta’s passage. But the SC denied this specific challenge and upheld the procedural validity of the law.
It found that Congress complied with the constitutional requirements in passing a law, such as the three-reading rule under Article VI of the Constitution.

“The Court likewise upheld the President’s Certification of Urgency and recognized the authority of the Bicameral Conference Committee to reconcile differences between the House and Senate versions of the proposed legislation,” the SC added. – Rappler.com
